steps.title: Make yourself at home
steps.body: Sit roughly in front of the centre of your keyboard. Keep your feet supported and your elbows around key height. Select a piano tone on your CT-X870IN using its PIANO/ORGAN button; check the display for the piano sound. Play any key gently.
steps.cue: Your only goal: a comfortable position and a sound you like.
steps.task: I’m comfortable and have a piano sound

steps.title: Spot the black-key pattern
steps.body: Look across the keyboard. Black keys repeat in groups of TWO and THREE. Find three different groups of two. You do not need to memorise any note names yet.
steps.cue: Point to a group of two, then a group of three, on your real keyboard.
steps.task: I can find both black-key groups

steps.title: Find your first C
steps.body: Find a group of two black keys near the middle. The white key immediately to their LEFT is C. Middle C is called C4 in this app. On the standard untransposed 61-key layout, it is the third C from the left.
steps.cue: Play C gently three times. Listen to the demonstration if you like.
steps.task: I found C on my keyboard

steps.title: A tiny musical hello
steps.body: Starting at C, move right to the next white key, D, then the next, E. With your right hand, try thumb on C, index on D, and middle finger on E. Play slowly, then come back down.
steps.cue: C · D · E · D · C. There is no rush.
steps.task: I played my first five-note phrase

steps.title: Find C again
steps.body: Find a group of two black keys. Name the white keys around it: C on the left, D between the black keys, E on the right. Find these three keys near the middle of your keyboard.
steps.cue: Say the letter names out loud as you play.

steps.title: Give each finger a note
steps.body: Rest your right thumb on C, index finger on D, and middle finger on E. Curve your fingers naturally. Play one note at a time and release before the next.
steps.cue: Right hand: 1 · 2 · 3 · 2 · 1.

steps.title: Change the order
steps.body: Keep the same hand position. Play E, then C, then D, then E. Pause and repeat. Notice that your fingers can find notes without your whole hand moving.
steps.cue: Right hand: 3 · 1 · 2 · 3.

steps.title: Try it with fewer hints
steps.body: Look away from the laptop and find C–D–E on the keyboard. Play up and back down twice. If you lose your place, use the group of two black keys to start again.
steps.cue: Aim for two comfortable attempts, at your own speed.

steps.title: Meet F and G
steps.body: From E, move to the next white key, F, then G. F sits immediately to the left of a group of three black keys. Play C, D, E, F, G slowly.
steps.cue: Five neighbouring white keys: C · D · E · F · G.

steps.title: Settle your five fingers
steps.body: Place your right hand on C–D–E–F–G: fingers 1–2–3–4–5. Press each key gently. Your ring finger may feel less independent; give it time.
steps.cue: Play 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5, without forcing or stretching.

steps.title: Come back home
steps.body: Play G–F–E–D–C with fingers 5–4–3–2–1. Leave a little space between notes if that helps. Repeat from C to G and back.
steps.cue: The final C should feel like coming home.

steps.title: A little skipping game
steps.body: Play C–E–G–E–C. You skip over D and F. Keep your fingers resting near their keys; use thumb, middle finger, and little finger.
steps.cue: Right hand: 1 · 3 · 5 · 3 · 1.

steps.title: Listen to the tune
steps.body: Press “Play the example” and listen once to “Hot Cross Buns”. Notice that its opening repeats and that some notes last longer. Rest your hands for now: you do not need to play, name the notes, or work them out by ear. The next checkpoint gives you the exact keys and fingers.
steps.cue: Your task is only to get familiar with how the tune sounds. Humming is optional.

steps.title: Learn the first phrase
steps.body: Put your right thumb on middle C (C4), index finger on D4, and middle finger on E4. Play E with your middle finger, D with your index, then C with your thumb. Press E once and hold while counting “1, 2”; do the same for D; hold C while counting “1, 2, 3, 4”. Repeat E–D–C. You can pause between notes while finding the keys.
steps.cue: E: middle finger, 2 beats → D: index, 2 beats → C: thumb, 4 beats.

steps.title: Learn the second phrase
steps.body: Play four Cs, then four Ds, using one beat for each note. Finish with E–D–C, holding those notes as in the opening.
steps.cue: C C C C · D D D D · E— D— C——.

steps.title: Put your tune together
steps.body: Play the two opening phrases, then four Cs, four Ds, and the ending. Pause between sections if needed. You have learned a complete little melody.
steps.cue: Try one full run, then celebrate your first tune.

steps.title: Tap the pulse
steps.body: Turn on the metronome below. Tap your thigh with one finger on each click. Count 1–2–3–4, then begin again. Try four groups of four.
steps.cue: Listen for a few clicks before you join in.

steps.title: One note on each beat
steps.body: With the metronome at 60, play middle C on each click. Lift the key between presses. Keep the tapping feeling from the previous step.
steps.cue: C · C · C · C. Four even notes.

steps.title: Keep the beat while moving
steps.body: Play C–D–E–D, one note per click. Repeat the pattern. If moving fingers makes you rush, slow the tempo to 45 or 50.
steps.cue: The notes change; the pulse stays the same.

steps.title: Make your own steady ending
steps.body: Play C–D–E–G, then hold C for four clicks. Try it twice. Stop the metronome when you finish.
steps.cue: A steady slow version is the goal.

steps.title: Hold for two beats
steps.body: Play C and keep the key down while you count 1–2. Play D for 1–2, then E for 1–2. Listen to the demo to hear the length.
steps.cue: One key press lasts two beats.

steps.title: Mix one and two
steps.body: Play C for one beat, D for one, and E for two. Count “1, 2, 3–4”. Repeat without a long gap.
steps.cue: C · D · E— | C · D · E—.

steps.title: Hold for four
steps.body: Play G for four beats, then E for four, then C for four. Keep your finger on the key but your arm relaxed. Do not press harder to keep a note going.
steps.cue: Count all four beats for every note.

steps.title: Use the rhythm in a phrase
steps.body: Play C–D–E–G with the lengths shown below, then finish on C. Tap the pulse with your foot only if it feels comfortable.

steps.title: Leave room for silence
steps.body: Play C for a beat, then lift your finger and stay silent for a beat. Repeat. The dash in the note strip means a rest.
steps.cue: C · rest · C · rest.

steps.title: A question and an answer
steps.body: Play C–D–E, then rest for one beat. Answer with E–D–C and another rest. Keep the silent beat as long as the played beats.
steps.cue: Three notes, one silent beat.

steps.title: Meet three rhythm symbols
steps.body: A quarter note (♩) lasts one beat in our exercises. A half note (𝅗𝅥) lasts two, and a whole note (𝅝) lasts four. The beat counts under the demonstration notes give you the same information.
steps.cue: Play C for 1 beat, D for 1, E for 2, and C for 4.

steps.title: Keep counting through a rest
steps.body: Try this phrase twice. Release E before the rest, stay silent for two beats, and finish on C for four.

steps.title: Soft and a little louder
steps.body: With touch response enabled, play C gently three times. Then play three times with a slightly quicker key press. Listen to your own keyboard for the change; our guide demo is only a pitch reference.
steps.cue: Compare your own soft and moderately loud sound.

steps.title: Separate the notes
steps.body: Play C–D–E–F–G with a little space between notes. Release each key before the next. Keep the movement light rather than sharply poking the keys.
steps.cue: Think “little footsteps”.

steps.title: Connect the notes
steps.body: Now try the same notes smoothly. Release one as you press the next, without holding both for a long time. Slow down until the transitions feel comfortable.
steps.cue: Think “one gentle line”.

steps.title: Shape a musical sentence
steps.body: Play C–D–E–G–E–D–C. Start softly, let the middle grow slightly, and finish softly. There is no volume score: use your ears.
steps.cue: Make the last C sound like the end of a sentence.

steps.title: Listen to the opening
steps.body: Play the example to hear the first part of “Mary Had a Little Lamb”. Listen for the repeated notes and short pauses between musical phrases. Keep your hands relaxed; you are not expected to play along or identify any keys from the sound. The notes and finger positions will be provided for practice.
steps.cue: Listen once. The next checkpoint teaches the first phrase with the notes shown.

steps.title: The first line
steps.body: Play E–D–C–D, then E three times. Hold the final E for two beats. Practise until your hand can stay relaxed.

steps.title: The middle and ending
steps.body: First practise D–D–D, E–G–G. Then play the opening again and finish E–D–D–E–D–C. The demonstration here combines the middle and final line.
steps.cue: Slow down before the jump from E to G.

steps.title: Play the complete melody
steps.body: Join the opening, middle, and ending. If one transition trips you up, repeat just the two notes around it before another full try.
steps.cue: Take a breath before you start.

steps.title: Hear the opening
steps.body: Play the example and listen for repeated sounds and the rise and fall of the tune. Humming is optional. You do not need to find any keys yet: the next checkpoint gives you the notes E–E–F–G, G–F–E–D and tells you which fingers to use.
steps.cue: Just listen to this short opening. No guessing and no playing along yet.

steps.title: Practise the first half
steps.body: Play E–E–F–G, then G–F–E–D. Use fingers 3–3–4–5, 5–4–3–2. Keep each note the same length.
steps.cue: Two little groups of four notes.

steps.title: Practise the answer
steps.body: Play C–C–D–E, then E–D–D. The first E in the ending lasts one and a half beats, the following D half a beat, and the last D two beats. Listen slowly to copy that rhythm.

steps.title: Play the opening theme
steps.body: Join both halves. A half-beat note is shorter, not necessarily louder. You can practise the pitches freely before following the exact rhythm.
steps.cue: Your first Beethoven milestone: one complete opening phrase.

steps.title: Hear the opening first
steps.body: Play the example and listen to the opening of “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star”. This tune will use A, the white key immediately to the right of G. For now, only listen; you do not need to search for the notes. The next checkpoint shows C–C–G–G–A–A–G and helps you position your hand.
steps.cue: Notice that the last sound is held longer. You will play in the next checkpoint.

steps.title: Play the opening and answer
steps.body: Practise the opening with fingers 1–1–4–4–5–5–4 if comfortable. Then settle back into the C–G position for F–F–E–E–D–D–C.
steps.cue: Move your hand gently instead of holding a wide stretch.

steps.title: The middle section
steps.body: Play G–G–F–F–E–E–D, holding D for two beats. Repeat that phrase. Use the familiar C–G hand position.
steps.cue: The middle is the same phrase twice.
steps.handGuide: Right hand: thumb (1) on C4, index (2) on D4, middle (3) on E4, ring (4) on F4, little finger (5) on G4.

steps.title: Put all three sections together
steps.body: Play the opening and answer, the middle section, then the opening and answer again. Breaks between sections are fine while learning.
steps.cue: Opening → middle → opening again.

steps.title: Complete the alphabet
steps.body: After G come A and B, then the names start again at C. Say C–D–E–F–G–A–B–C while playing with any comfortable finger. This is a note map, not a scale-fingering exercise.
steps.cue: There is no H in our note alphabet.

steps.title: Find the same name elsewhere
steps.body: Find a C to the left of middle C, then middle C, then the C to its right. We call these C3, C4, and C5. Higher numbers mean higher pitches.
steps.cue: Hear the same note family at three heights.

steps.title: Meet a black-key name
steps.body: The black key immediately to the right of C is C-sharp, written C♯. It can also be called D-flat, D♭. Today just find it and compare C–C♯–D.
steps.cue: Sharp means one key higher, including black keys.

steps.title: Move a familiar phrase up
steps.body: Play E–D–C near middle C, then find E–D–C one octave higher. Listen to how the tune stays recognisable.
steps.cue: Same letter pattern, a different height.

steps.title: Find the three notes
steps.body: Place your right thumb on C, middle finger on E, and little finger on G. Play the notes separately first.
steps.cue: C · E · G. Fingers 1 · 3 · 5.

steps.title: Play them together
steps.body: Press C, E, and G at the same time. Hold for four beats, then release all three. Try it three times, letting your hand relax between attempts.
steps.cue: A plus sign means “play together”: C + E + G.

steps.title: Give your chord a pulse
steps.body: Play the C chord once every two beats. Count 1–2 between presses. Keep the notes balanced instead of striking one much harder.
steps.cue: Play, hold · play, hold.

steps.title: Recognise the sound
steps.body: Compare C–E–G played separately with the same notes together. Try the separate notes first and the chord second without looking at the screen.
steps.cue: You can now play your first major chord.

steps.title: Build A minor
steps.body: Find A below middle C. With your right hand, try thumb on A3, middle finger on C4, little finger on E4. Play separately, then together.
steps.cue: Am = A + C + E.

steps.title: Build F major
steps.body: Find F below middle C. Place your right fingers 1–3–5 on F3–A3–C4. Play separately, then together.
steps.cue: F = F + A + C.

steps.title: Move slowly between them
steps.body: Play Am, release, and take two silent beats to move to F. Look at the destination before moving. You can take longer than the demo.
steps.cue: Am → a comfortable move → F.

steps.title: Try a three-chord journey
steps.body: Play C major, A minor, and F major, holding each for four beats. Pause to reposition when needed. Say each chord name as you play.
steps.cue: C → Am → F.

steps.title: Meet G major
steps.body: With your right hand, find G3–B3–D4. Use fingers 1–3–5 if comfortable. Play the three notes separately, then together.
steps.cue: G = G + B + D.

steps.title: Move from C to G
steps.body: Play C major for four beats, then release and find G major. Practise the move without a metronome first. Repeat with a steady pulse when ready.
steps.cue: Give your eyes time to find the next shape.

steps.title: Four chords, slowly
steps.body: Try C–G–Am–F. Hold each for four beats. Keep the pace slow enough that you can find the next shape without tensing your wrist.
steps.cue: C → G → Am → F.

steps.title: Repeat with a steady pulse
steps.body: Loop the demonstration and practise the four-chord sequence. Aim for two relaxed rounds. If a change is difficult, practise only that pair.
steps.cue: A clean change at 40 BPM is progress.

steps.title: Open up a C chord
steps.body: Play C–E–G–E with fingers 1–3–5–3. Give each note one beat. Use the same relaxed position as your C-major chord.
steps.cue: C · E · G · E.

steps.title: Try A minor
steps.body: Move to A3–C4–E4. Play A–C–E–C with fingers 1–3–5–3. Keep all four notes evenly spaced.
steps.cue: A · C · E · C.

steps.title: Try F and G
steps.body: Play F–A–C–A, then G–B–D–B. Release and reposition between patterns. Add a pause if that makes the transition more comfortable.
steps.cue: F · A · C · A | G · B · D · B.

steps.title: Make a flowing little loop
steps.body: Join C, Am, F, and G broken chords. Loop slowly. This original exercise prepares you for flowing pop accompaniments, including the kind of coordination you will need for Adele.
steps.cue: Even notes first; speed can come later.

steps.title: Choose your chord colours
steps.body: Open the chord playground and select C, Am, F, and G in turn. Find the highlighted notes on your Casio, then play each chord with your right thumb, middle finger, and little finger. Pick two chords whose sounds you enjoy together.
steps.cue: Try C → Am first. Hear the difference, then make your own choice.
steps.task: I explored the four chord shapes

steps.title: Build a four-chord story
steps.body: In the playground, choose a chord for each of the four bars. A bar here is a group of four beats. Try C–G–Am–F, then change the order. Select “Hold the chord” and play each shape for four beats. Pauses to find the next shape are fine.
steps.cue: Try the same four chords in a new order. Which ending do you prefer?
steps.task: I chose and played my own four-bar sequence

steps.title: One sequence, two different feels
steps.body: Keep your chosen chord order. Try “Give it a pulse”: press each chord on beats 1 and 3. Then try “Let it ripple”: play the lowest, middle, highest, and middle notes separately. Practise one chord at a time before joining the sequence.
steps.cue: The chord notes stay the same; the rhythm and movement change.
steps.task: I tried pulsing and broken chords

steps.title: Your mini performance
steps.body: Choose the playing style you enjoyed most. Play your four-bar sequence twice, beginning softly and finishing on a held chord. You can hum a little tune over it if you like. The demonstration is an example; your own chord order is welcome.
steps.cue: Your playground sequence and speed save automatically. Come back and make another version anytime.
steps.task: I played a short piece of my own

steps.title: Find a lower C
steps.body: Find C3, one octave below middle C. Place your left little finger on it. Play C three times, leaving your wrist relaxed.
steps.cue: Left hand, finger 5, lower C.

steps.title: Five notes in the left hand
steps.body: Place left fingers 5–4–3–2–1 on C3–D3–E3–F3–G3. Play up and back down slowly.
steps.cue: The finger numbers decrease as the notes rise.

steps.title: Practise bass-note moves
steps.body: Use any comfortable left-hand fingers to play C3, G3, A3, F3. Hold each for four beats. Move your whole hand when needed.
steps.cue: These are the root notes of C, G, Am, and F.

steps.title: Keep a slow left-hand pulse
steps.body: Repeat the bass-note sequence twice with the metronome at 50. Press each note on beat 1 and hold through beat 4.
steps.cue: One note per four clicks.

steps.title: Prepare each hand
steps.body: Put left little finger on C3 and right thumb on C4. Play left C, then right C, alternating slowly.
steps.cue: Low C · middle C · low C · middle C.

steps.title: Land together
steps.body: Press both Cs at the same time, hold for two beats, and release together. Repeat with a short rest between attempts.
steps.cue: One key per hand. One shared start.

steps.title: Hold left, move right
steps.body: Hold left C3 for four beats. While it stays down, play right C4, D4, E4, D4, one per beat. The demo retriggers the bass at the beginning only.
steps.cue: Left: hold C. Right: C · D · E · D.

steps.title: Repeat your first two-hand phrase
steps.body: Try the same four-beat pattern twice. Release both hands between rounds. If needed, return to separate hands, then try together again.
steps.cue: Aim for two comfortable rounds, however slowly.

steps.title: Build a full C sound
steps.body: Play C3 with your left hand and C4–E4–G4 together with your right. Hold for four beats. Release and repeat.
steps.cue: Left: C. Right: C major.

steps.title: Add A minor
steps.body: Play A3 with the left hand and A4–C5–E5 with the right. Take time to find the new position. Play both hands together for four beats.
steps.cue: Left: A. Right: A minor.

steps.title: Explore F and G
steps.body: For F, use left F3 and right F4–A4–C5. For G, use left G3 and right G4–B4–D5. Try each separately before moving between them.
steps.cue: A single low note supports each full chord.

steps.title: Your first accompaniment
steps.body: Play C–Am–F–G using a left root and right chord. The hands move to matching letter roots. Leave extra time between changes if needed.
steps.cue: One chord per four beats. Feel how much sound two hands can make.

steps.title: Practise the right-hand pattern
steps.body: Play C4–E4–G4–E4 in the right hand. Repeat slowly until you can think about the pattern instead of searching for each key.

steps.title: Add one held bass note
steps.body: Press left C3 with the first right C4. Hold left C3 while the right hand continues E4–G4–E4. Release after four beats.
steps.cue: Left stays down; right keeps moving.

steps.title: Try the same idea on F
steps.body: Hold left F3. With the right hand, play F4–A4–C5–A4. Practise this shape alone before moving from C.
steps.cue: Same rhythm, different chord notes.

steps.title: Switch after a breathing space
steps.body: Play one C pattern, rest and find F, then play one F pattern. For this transition drill, the demo uses shorter bass notes. On your keyboard, hold each bass through its four-note pattern.
steps.cue: C pattern → pause → F pattern.

steps.title: Listen for the job of the keyboard
steps.body: Play the example to hear our original repeating-chord exercise. Just notice its steady pulse; you are not expected to name the chords or copy them by ear. Optionally listen to your own recording of “The Scientist” to hear how its piano part supports the voice. Our exercise is not the song; the next checkpoint shows exactly which chord notes to play.
steps.cue: Listen now. Follow the provided chord notes when you reach the playing checkpoint.

steps.title: Repeat a chord without rushing
steps.body: Play a C chord on beats 1 and 3 of a four-beat count. Keep the two presses equal in volume. Repeat with Am.
steps.cue: Count 1–2–3–4. Play on 1 and 3.

steps.title: Change the shape on time
steps.body: Practise C–Am–F–G, playing each chord twice. This general progression is a technique drill, not the song’s progression. Slow down at the hardest transition.
steps.cue: Two presses per chord, no hurry between shapes.

steps.title: Make it sound like a phrase
steps.body: Play the drill softly once, then a little fuller. Keep the tempo the same. Your milestone is a steady accompaniment pattern you can repeat comfortably.
steps.cue: Feel the phrase, keep the pulse.

steps.title: Revisit bass plus chord
steps.body: Play left C3 with right C4–E4–G4. Hold for four beats and release. Then do the same with F3 and F4–A4–C5.
steps.cue: Start both hands together.

steps.title: Repeat the right-hand chord
steps.body: For this drill, press the left root and right chord together on beats 1 and 3. Once that feels comfortable, try holding the left note through all four beats while repeating only the right chord.
steps.cue: First coordinate the starts; then experiment with a held bass.

steps.title: Build a four-chord accompaniment
steps.body: Try C–Am–F–G with both hands, one press per four beats. Use the highlighted keys as a map. Work on a single change if the whole loop feels too much.
steps.cue: Keep the left hand simple and the tempo gentle.

steps.title: Choose your next song step
steps.body: Try two comfortable rounds. Then use a beginner arrangement of “The Scientist” that you own or can legally access. Start with only its first two chords, checking its key and fingering rather than assuming this drill matches.
steps.cue: You have built a foundation for learning the real arrangement.

steps.title: Hear a repeating shape
steps.body: Play the example to hear our original flowing-note exercise. Listen to the even spacing between sounds. You do not need to identify the notes by ear or play along yet; the next checkpoint gives you C–E–G–E and the fingers to use. Optionally listen to “Someone Like You” separately to notice its flowing accompaniment. This exercise is not a transcription of the song.
steps.cue: Listen only: one gentle sound on each beat. The keys are provided when you practise.

steps.title: Keep four notes even
steps.body: Play C–E–G–E repeatedly with fingers 1–3–5–3. Keep your thumb from landing noticeably louder. Stop and relax between rounds.
steps.cue: An even sound matters more than speed.

steps.title: Move the repeating pattern
steps.body: Play C–E–G–E, then A–C–E–C below it. Practise the move without the metronome before adding a slow pulse.
steps.cue: C pattern → Am pattern.

steps.title: Find a comfortable flow
steps.body: Join C, Am, F, and G broken chords. This is an original practice progression. Loop it slowly, then try without looking at the screen for the first pattern.
steps.cue: Let each four-note shape feel familiar.

steps.title: Start with one chord and two hands
steps.body: Hold left C3 for four beats while the right plays C4–E4–G4–E4. Try it twice, resting between rounds.
steps.cue: One held bass; four even right-hand notes.

steps.title: Try an A-minor shape
steps.body: Hold left A3. Play right A4–C5–E5–C5. Work on this shape alone first. Give yourself time to position both hands.
steps.cue: Let the left hand stay quiet while the right moves.

steps.title: Make your own short performance
steps.body: Choose either our C pattern or Am pattern. Play it four times with a steady, comfortable pulse. Start gently and finish deliberately. You can loop this C demonstration or revisit the previous step for Am.
steps.cue: One simple pattern played with care is music.

steps.title: Your next chapter
steps.body: Choose a beginner arrangement of “Someone Like You” that you own or can legally access. Begin with one small right-hand pattern, then its bass note. Use the same listen → separate hands → combine → repeat approach. Keep revisiting the drills that help.
steps.cue: Celebrate: you have explored notes, rhythm, tunes, chords, and both hands.
steps.task: Finish the foundations course

steps.title: Find B-flat
steps.body: Find the group of three black keys near middle C. B-flat (B♭) is the rightmost black key in that group, immediately to the left of B. Play A4, B♭4, and B4 slowly. B♭ and A♯ are two names for this same key; we use B♭ in this song.
steps.cue: Find the key first; the demonstration is an original note-finding exercise.
steps.handGuide: Right hand: try thumb on A4, index on B♭4, middle on B4. Keep your fingers relaxed.

steps.title: Walk through the song’s note family
steps.body: Try F4–G4–A4–B♭4, then pause and reposition for C5–D5–E5–F5. This introduces the F-major note family. You do not need to learn a fast scale or thumb crossing now. Notice that B is flat, while the other letters here are white keys.
steps.cue: Two groups of four, with a pause to move your hand.
steps.handGuide: Right hand: 1–2–3–4 for each group. Release, move, then begin the next group with your thumb.

steps.title: Move without holding a stretch
steps.body: Play C4, F4, and A4 separately. Release, then try them together if the shape feels comfortable. Do the same with D4, F4, and B♭4. Never keep your thumb pinned down while reaching. These two shapes prepare the chord changes in the next lesson.
steps.cue: Release → move → find the next shape.
steps.handGuide: Right hand: try 1–3–5 for C–F–A and 1–2–5 for D–F–B♭. Play notes separately if the reach is uncomfortable.

steps.title: Find the bass notes
steps.body: With your left hand, find D3, B♭3, and F3. Our starter exercises use B♭3 above F3 to stay within the displayed keyboard. This changes the bass register from some arrangements, while keeping the same harmony. Find each note before trying to change on a beat.
steps.cue: D → B♭ → F → F. One note at a time.
steps.handGuide: Left hand: use any comfortable finger, releasing and moving your hand between bass notes. B♭3 is just below middle C.

steps.title: Build D minor seven across your hands
steps.body: Play D3 with your left hand. Place your right thumb on C4, middle finger on F4, and little finger on A4. Together, the four notes form D minor seven (Dm7). First find each note, then press both hands together. The right-hand shape alone is an F chord; the low D supplies the Dm7 sound.
steps.cue: Left: D. Right: C–F–A. Find the notes before adding rhythm.
steps.task: I found both hand positions and played them comfortably.

steps.title: Make the B-flat shape
steps.body: Release the previous shape. Play left B♭3 and right D4–F4–B♭4. Try right fingers 1–2–5. Keep F as a visual landmark, but let your hand release and reposition freely. Practise the change from the previous checkpoint without a metronome first.
steps.cue: Two B-flat keys: one in each hand.
steps.task: I can find the B♭ shape without a strained reach.

steps.title: Meet F and its suspended neighbour
steps.body: For F, play left F3 and right C4–F4–A4. For Fsus2, keep the left F and change the top right-hand note from A4 to G4. Try 1–3–5 for F and 1–3–4 for Fsus2. “Sus2” describes this change in chord colour; you do not need to memorise the theory yet.
steps.cue: Right-hand top note: A → G. Keep the movement small.
steps.task: I heard and played the difference between F and Fsus2.

steps.title: Join the four shapes slowly
steps.body: Move through Dm7, B♭, F, and Fsus2, allowing a full four-count for each. These are the song’s main opening and verse harmonies. This is a simplified chord study: it does not contain the sung melody or every detail of the recording. Pause between shapes until they feel familiar.
steps.cue: Four shapes, then a rest. Aim for comfortable changes.
steps.task: I can move through the four shapes twice with comfortable pauses.

steps.title: Hold left, repeat right
steps.body: Select “Right hand” and hear four gentle chord presses. Then select “Left hand” and hear one held bass note. Finally choose “Both hands”. On your Casio, hold the left note while the right repeats. Start after the four count-in clicks; the count-in returns at the start of every loop.
steps.cue: Left hand holds; right hand presses once per beat.
steps.task: I kept the bass down while playing four even right-hand presses.

steps.title: Make one change on the next first beat
steps.body: Work on just Dm7 to B♭. Practise the hands separately, then together at 40–50 BPM. Move into the new shape on the next “1”. The bar-range controls let you repeat either bar or the pair. You can stop the example and practise at your own pace.
steps.cue: Count 1–2–3–4, then change on 1.
steps.task: I changed both hands together without rushing the last beat.

steps.title: Keep the whole loop steady
steps.body: Use the four-bar chord study. Keep the left hand to one held note per bar and the right to one press per beat. Choose only the bars around a difficult change, then widen the range. Repeat at a comfortable speed; 76 BPM is a later reference tempo, not today’s requirement.
steps.cue: A slow steady loop is enough.
steps.task: I played the four-bar study twice with a steady count.

steps.title: Optional: two left taps for each right press
steps.body: This optional coordination exercise uses repeated D notes in the left hand while the right repeats a chord. Count “1-and-2-and-3-and-4-and”: left on every number and “and”, right on numbers only. Practise tapping first. This prepares a busier accompaniment; the simple held-bass version is enough for your first song milestone.
steps.cue: Try the extra pulse only if the simpler version feels relaxed.
steps.task: I explored the faster left-hand pulse, or chose the held-bass version for now.

steps.title: Read upward from middle C
steps.body: Open the note map below. The five-line staff is a picture of higher and lower notes. Middle C sits on a short extra line below it; D sits in the gap above C, and E on the bottom staff line. Follow this original C–D–E exercise while looking between the map and your keyboard.
steps.cue: Higher on the page means farther right on the keyboard.

steps.title: Find the notes above E
steps.body: On the treble staff, the lines from bottom to top are E–G–B–D–F; the spaces are F–A–C–E. The B-flat sign at the beginning of the song score tells you to play B-flat whenever B appears, unless another sign changes it. Use the note map whenever needed; this is not a memory test.
steps.cue: Follow the position, then check the B-flat reminder.

steps.title: Count short sounds and space
steps.body: A filled note with a stem usually lasts one beat here. A flag or beam makes it half a beat: count a number and “and” across each pair. A hollow note with a stem lasts two beats. A rest means leave space; a curved tie between the same pitch means keep holding, not press again. Tap this original exercise before playing it.
steps.cue: C on 1-and, D on 2, silence on 3, E on 4.

steps.title: Find your starting place in the song
steps.body: Open Pianote’s score using the button below. Page 1 begins with the chord introduction. The sung melody starts in the system marked 6. Follow the top lyric row for verse one, but use the staff for the notes. Locate bars 6–9 before playing; this is the first short-section target. A bar number is a location in this specific score, not a finger or beat count.
steps.cue: Reference checkpoint: open the score and find bars 6–9.

reference.location: Page 1 · system beginning at bar 6 · top lyric row

steps.task: I found the first melody section in the reference.

steps.title: First phrase: take only bar 6
steps.body: Keep Pianote’s score open at bar 6 on page 1. Ignore the chord symbols for now: use only the single-note melody and the top lyric row. Locate each note using the map, tap its rhythm, then play with your right hand. Keep the opening rest. Stop at the bar line, even if you want to continue.
steps.cue: One bar only. Find notes → tap → play → repeat.

reference.location: Page 1 · bar 6 · opening rest and first melody phrase

steps.task: I can play the first small phrase slowly twice.

steps.title: Second phrase: work on bar 7
steps.body: Move to bar 7 in the same system. Find the notes and rhythm before playing. Practise it alone, then join the last part of bar 6 to the start of bar 7. A pause to find your hand position is fine while learning; gradually shorten that pause. Use the original recording or source demonstration to check the phrasing.
steps.cue: Practise the join as well as the new notes.
steps.task: I can play the second phrase and join it to the first.

steps.title: Third phrase: finish bars 8–9
steps.body: Learn bar 8 and the first ending at bar 9. Follow the top lyric row and the ending marked for the early repeats. Work on pitches first, then keep the longer ending note for its full written length. Stop here: the later alternate ending belongs to a later verse repetition.
steps.cue: Let the end of the phrase breathe.
steps.task: I can play the third phrase with its held ending.

steps.title: Save your first song milestone
steps.body: Join bars 6–9 using the top lyric row and first ending. Play right hand only at a speed where you can keep going. Aim for two recognisable rounds with the rests and held notes in place. This is a short section of the actual melody, not completion of the whole song. If a join interrupts you, save this lesson for more practice and revisit that pair of bars.
steps.cue: Your first milestone: three connected melody chunks.
steps.task: I played the opening section twice with my right hand.

steps.title: Practise only the bass changes
steps.body: For the short verse section, prepare one bass note for each main harmony: D, B♭, F, then F again. Use the chord symbols above the source melody to locate each change. This bass-only study gives you a simple starting accompaniment; it does not play the melody for you.
steps.cue: Left hand alone before trying the melody above it.
steps.task: I can find each bass note at a slow four-count.

steps.title: Add the bass to the first phrase
steps.body: Return to bar 6. Put your left hand on the bass note for its chord and your right hand ready for the melody. Start the bass on the bar’s first beat, then enter the melody after its written rest. Hold the bass while the melody moves. Practise this small section alone; leave out the bass temporarily if it interrupts the melody.
steps.cue: The bass can start before the melody does.

reference.location: Page 1 · bar 6 · bass on beat 1, melody after its rest

steps.task: I can hold a bass note while playing the first melody phrase.

steps.title: Join the next two phrases
steps.body: Add the bass changes to bars 7–9. Use one left-hand note at each chord change, holding it while your right hand plays the melody. At first, pause before each new bar to place both hands. Then practise only the last beat before a change and the first beat after it.
steps.cue: Keep the left hand simpler than the melody.

reference.location: Page 1 · bars 7–9 · chord changes above the melody

steps.task: I joined the remaining phrases with simple bass notes.

steps.title: Play your short section with both hands
steps.body: Play the opening section, bars 6–9, with right-hand melody and one left bass note per chord change. Listen for the melody clearly above the bass; press the left notes gently. Two comfortable rounds count as the milestone. A pedal and the recording’s faster left-hand rhythm are optional later refinements.
steps.cue: A recognisable section, two hands, your own pace.

reference.location: Page 1 · bars 6–9 · melody plus simple bass

steps.task: I played the short song section with both hands twice.

steps.title: Find the chorus entrance
steps.body: On page 1, find the chorus starting at bar 11. Learn the first small phrase with the right hand alone. Notice its entry and held notes rather than forcing every note onto a click. Use the note map and source rhythm; the opening verse melody is not a substitute for this section.
steps.cue: New melody, familiar practice method.
steps.task: I can play the first chorus phrase with my right hand.

steps.title: Learn the chorus in pairs of bars
steps.body: Continue through the chorus in two-bar pieces. Follow the repeat endings in the source: a repeated opening can lead to a different ending. Practise each ending separately, then practise the turn into it. Add a simple bass only after the melody feels familiar.
steps.cue: Mark where the second ending differs before joining it.

reference.location: Page 1 · bars 11–17 · chorus phrases and endings

steps.task: I can connect the chorus phrases and choose the correct ending.

steps.title: Prepare the C harmony
steps.body: The return from the chorus introduces C harmony. Practise a plain C-major chord with a low C, then move to Dm7. This original transition study isolates the hand movement. When applying it to the song, follow the reference for the actual duration and melody rather than copying this study’s two-bar timing.
steps.cue: C is familiar. Practise the move back to Dm7.
steps.task: I can find C and move into the next chord comfortably.

steps.title: Join the chorus to the next section
steps.body: Work through the chorus ending and the instrumental return. First practise the last two bars of the chorus, then the first two bars of the following section. Join them without restarting the whole song. If the instrumental texture is difficult, use the chord symbols to play a simple bass-and-chord version.
steps.cue: Practise the doorway between sections.

reference.location: Page 1 · bars 18–24 · chorus ending and instrumental return

steps.task: I can finish the chorus and enter the next section.

steps.title: Complete the first verse
steps.body: Return to the first verse and follow each lyric row and its repeat ending in the reference. Your opening short section is the starting point; later rows can change the rhythm or phrase ending. Practise those differences instead of assuming every repeat is identical. Then join the complete verse to the chorus.
steps.cue: Reuse what is familiar; practise the changed endings.

reference.location: Page 1 · first verse repeats and transition into the chorus

steps.task: I played the first verse and reached the chorus.

steps.title: Learn the second verse
steps.body: On page 2, locate the second verse beginning in the system marked 25. Use the same method: one phrase, two phrases, then a longer section. Check the new rhythm carefully. Keep the left hand to simple bass notes until the right-hand line is comfortable.
steps.cue: Similar harmony does not mean every melody rhythm is identical.

reference.location: Page 2 · second verse, systems marked 25 and 28

steps.task: I can play the second verse in connected phrases.

steps.title: Practise the repeat route
steps.body: Follow the second verse into the returning chorus. The score’s D.S. al Coda tells you to return to the marked sign and later jump at “To coda” to the ending marked CODA. Trace that route with your finger before playing. If repeats feel confusing, use the song-map checklist below to track the sections in performance order.
steps.cue: Trace the route first; then practise its transitions.

reference.location: Page 2 · D.S. al Coda, returning chorus, and coda

steps.task: I know which section comes next through the repeats.

steps.title: Give the song a deliberate ending
steps.body: Work on the final instrumental/vocal ending on page 2. Use the reference’s indicated repeats, then its final bars. You may simplify the accompaniment to held bass and chords while keeping the melody clear. Practise the last phrase by itself; slow and release deliberately at the end instead of stopping abruptly.
steps.cue: Learn how to finish, not just how to begin.
steps.task: I can play the ending and release the final sound deliberately.

steps.title: Opening through the first chorus
steps.body: Prepare your reference and choose a comfortable tempo. Play a simple chord introduction, then verse one and the first chorus. Keep the right-hand melody and simple left bass as your arrangement. Use the song map to stay oriented. Note a difficult transition and practise just that join before another run.
steps.cue: Introduction → verse one → chorus.

reference.location: Page 1 · opening, verse one, and first chorus

steps.task: I connected the opening, first verse and chorus.

steps.title: The middle of your song
steps.body: Start from the instrumental return rather than the beginning. Continue into verse two and the returning chorus. Practise starting at this middle point so a mistake does not force you to restart the entire performance. Keep the accompaniment at the same simple level throughout.
steps.cue: Instrumental return → verse two → returning chorus.

reference.location: Pages 1–2 · instrumental return and second verse/chorus route

steps.task: I can start from the middle and continue through the chorus.

steps.title: Connect the last transition
steps.body: Practise the final chorus transition into the ending, following the coda route. Begin two bars before the transition and continue two bars beyond it. Then play the whole final section. Pedal is optional: clear releases and balanced hands are enough for this simplified version.
steps.cue: Final chorus → instrumental ending → final release.
steps.task: I can reach and finish the ending without restarting.

steps.title: Save a complete performance
steps.body: Play from the introduction through both verses, the choruses, the instrumental links and the ending. Use the source and song map as much as you need. Keep a steady comfortable tempo; small mistakes are fine if you recover. Mark this checkpoint only after playing the complete simplified arrangement. Completing the earlier chord studies alone does not meet this milestone.
steps.cue: The goal is a whole simplified performance—not matching every detail of the studio recording.

reference.location: Both reference pages · whole simplified arrangement

steps.task: I played the complete simplified song from beginning to end.

steps.title: Hear which way the sound moves
steps.body: Press “Play the mystery” to hear two notes. Decide whether the second sound goes higher, lower, or stays the same. You do not need to name it yet. Listen again, hum the two sounds if comfortable, and then reveal the answer. This lesson intentionally hides the notes: it is different from the earlier guided lessons.
steps.cue: Start with the direction of the sound, not a whole song.
steps.hint: The first sound is middle C. Hear that reference, then notice whether the second sound feels above or below it.
steps.answer: It goes higher: C4 → E4. On the keyboard, E is to the right of C.
steps.task: I compared the direction and checked the answer

steps.title: Find one note from three choices
steps.body: Play the mystery note, then try C4, D4, and E4 on your Casio one at a time. Replay the mystery between attempts. Which key sounds like the same pitch? Keep the keyboard on a piano tone at its standard pitch; the guide and Casio may have different tone colours. Reveal the answer when you want to compare.
steps.cue: Your possible keys are C4, D4, and E4. Take your time comparing them.
steps.hint: Compare the mystery with middle C. It is one white-key step higher.
steps.answer: The note is D4. Use your right index finger if your thumb is resting on C4.
steps.task: I tried the candidate keys and checked my match

steps.title: Find a three-note phrase
steps.body: This mystery starts on middle C and uses only C4, D4, and E4. Listen to all three sounds, then replay and find the second sound before adding the third. Use your right thumb, index, and middle finger on C, D, and E. You can hear the starting note separately or open a hint. Reveal the notes after your attempt.
steps.cue: Start at the given C. Find the next sound, then the next; pauses are welcome.
steps.hint: From C, the phrase skips up to the highest of your three keys, then steps down one white key.
steps.answer: C4 → E4 → D4. Right hand: thumb (1) → middle (3) → index (2). Each note lasts two beats.
steps.task: I tried finding the phrase and compared it with the answer

steps.title: Work out the opening of a tune
steps.body: Listen to this short melody without the note guide. It starts on E4 and uses only C4, D4, and E4. Hum it if helpful. Find the first three notes on your Casio, then add the next few. Work on the pitches first and the rhythm afterward. You may recognise it from an earlier lesson; remembering is helpful, but compare what you play with what you hear.
steps.cue: This is one short song phrase, not a test of working out a full arrangement.
steps.hint: It starts with three descending notes, climbs back to its starting note, then repeats that note. The final sound lasts two beats.
steps.answer: The opening of “Mary Had a Little Lamb”: E4 → D4 → C4 → D4 → E4 → E4 → E4. Fingers: 3–2–1–2–3–3–3. All notes last one beat except the final E, held for two.
steps.task: I explored a song phrase by ear and checked it
